statement: Taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried primarily by which nerve?
optionExplanations: Glossopharyngeal nerve: Carries taste and general sensation from the posterior one-third of the tongue.
Lingual nerve: Carries general somatic sensation, not taste, from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
Chorda tympani is the correct answer.
Hypoglossal nerve: Provides motor supply to most intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue.
Greater petrosal nerve: Carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers mainly to the pterygopalatine ganglion.
citation:
C. Chorda tympani

Explanation

Why C is correct:
The chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve carries special visceral afferent taste fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. These fibers travel with the lingual nerve before joining the facial nerve.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Glossopharyngeal nerve: Carries taste and general sensation from the posterior one-third of the tongue.

B. Lingual nerve: Carries general somatic sensation, not taste, from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

statement: Taeniae coli are characteristic longitudinal bands of smooth muscle found on which part of the gastrointestinal tract?
optionExplanations: Esophagus: The esophageal muscular wall has continuous circular and longitudinal layers without taeniae coli.
Stomach: The stomach has three continuous muscle layers rather than three taeniae.
Jejunum: The jejunum has continuous smooth-muscle layers and no taeniae coli.
Colon is the correct answer.
Rectum below the rectosigmoid junction: The taeniae spread out to form a continuous longitudinal layer at the rectosigmoid junction.
citation:
D. Colon

Explanation

The colon has three longitudinal smooth-muscle bands called taeniae coli. Their shorter length relative to the colon produces the sacculations known as haustra.

B. Stomach: The stomach has three continuous muscle layers rather than three taeniae.

statement: Meckel diverticulum results from persistence of which embryonic structure?
optionExplanations: Urachus: Persistence of the urachus causes a urachal fistula, sinus, or cyst.
Vitelline duct is the correct answer.
Allantois: The allantois contributes to the urachus and does not form Meckel diverticulum.
Dorsal mesogastrium: The dorsal mesogastrium contributes to peritoneal ligaments and the greater omentum.
Left umbilical vein: The left umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres of the liver after birth.
citation:
B. Vitelline duct

Explanation

Why B is correct:
Meckel diverticulum is caused by persistence of the proximal vitelline, or omphalomesenteric, duct that once connected the embryonic midgut to the yolk sac.

Why the other options are incorrect:

C. Allantois: The allantois contributes to the urachus and does not form Meckel diverticulum.

D. Dorsal mesogastrium: The dorsal mesogastrium contributes to peritoneal ligaments and the greater omentum.

E. Left umbilical vein: The left umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres of the liver after birth.

coreConcept: First pharyngeal arch contribution to tongue
statement: The lateral lingual swellings that form most of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue are derived from which pharyngeal arch?

Second pharyngeal arch: The second arch is overgrown during tongue development and does not form the adult mucosal surface.
Third pharyngeal arch: The third arch forms most of the posterior one-third of the tongue.

A. First pharyngeal arch

The two lateral lingual swellings arise from the first pharyngeal arch and overgrow the tuberculum impar to form most of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

coreConcept: Midgut rotation around the superior mesenteric artery
statement: During normal embryologic development, the midgut rotates around the axis of which artery?
optionExplanations: Celiac trunk: The celiac trunk supplies foregut derivatives and is not the axis of midgut rotation.
Superior mesenteric artery is the correct answer.
Inferior mesenteric artery: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies hindgut derivatives.
Common hepatic artery: The common hepatic artery is a branch of the celiac trunk.
Splenic artery: The splenic artery supplies foregut-derived organs and is not the rotational axis.
citation:
B. Superior mesenteric artery

Explanation

Why B is correct:
The midgut loop undergoes a total counterclockwise rotation of 270 degrees around the superior mesenteric artery.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Celiac trunk: The celiac trunk supplies foregut derivatives and is not the axis of midgut rotation.

C. Inferior mesenteric artery: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies hindgut derivatives.

coreConcept: Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium of gingiva
statement: Healthy gingiva is predominantly lined by which type of epithelium?
optionExplanations: Simple columnar epithelium: Simple columnar epithelium lines much of the gastrointestinal tract, not the gingiva.
Nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium: Nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium lines flexible oral regions such as the inner lips and cheeks.
Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium is the correct answer.
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium: Pseudostratified ciliated epithelium is typical of the respiratory tract.
Transitional epithelium: Transitional epithelium lines the urinary collecting system.
citation:
C. Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium

Explanation

Why C is correct:
The masticatory mucosa covering the gingiva and hard palate is lined mainly by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, which resists friction during chewing.

Why the other options are incorrect:

coreConcept: Volvulus due to abnormal midgut rotation
statement: A neonate develops bilious vomiting because abnormal midgut rotation has left a narrow mesenteric base that twists around the superior mesenteric artery. What is this complication called?
optionExplanations: Intussusception: Intussusception is telescoping of one bowel segment into another.
Volvulus is the correct answer.
Omphalocele: Omphalocele is persistence of herniated abdominal contents within a membrane-covered umbilical sac.
Gastroschisis: Gastroschisis is extrusion of bowel through an abdominal-wall defect without a covering membrane.
Meconium ileus: Meconium ileus is obstruction by thick meconium, classically in cystic fibrosis.
citation:
B. Volvulus

Explanation

Why B is correct:
Abnormal rotation and fixation can leave the midgut suspended on a narrow vascular pedicle. Twisting of the bowel around this pedicle produces a midgut volvulus and may compromise its blood supply.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Intussusception: Intussusception is telescoping of one bowel segment into another.

C. Omphalocele: Omphalocele is persistence of herniated abdominal contents within a membrane-covered umbilical sac.

D. Gastroschisis: Gastroschisis is extrusion of bowel through an abdominal-wall defect without a covering membrane.

coreConcept: Second part of duodenum and head of pancreas
statement: The second part of the duodenum curves around which structure?
optionExplanations: Body of pancreas: The pancreatic body extends leftward across the posterior abdominal wall.
Tail of pancreas: The pancreatic tail approaches the splenic hilum.
Head of pancreas is the correct answer.
Neck of pancreas: The neck lies anterior to the formation of the portal vein and is not encircled by the second part.
Uncinate process only: The uncinate process is part of the head but is not the complete structure enclosed by the duodenal curve.
citation:
C. Head of pancreas

Why C is correct:
The C-shaped duodenum embraces the head of the pancreas; its descending second part lies along the right side of the pancreatic head.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Body of pancreas: The pancreatic body extends leftward across the posterior abdominal wall.

B. Tail of pancreas: The pancreatic tail approaches the splenic hilum.

D. Neck of pancreas: The neck lies anterior to the formation of the portal vein and is not encircled by the second part.

E. Uncinate process only: The uncinate process is part of the head but is not the complete structure enclosed by the duodenal curve.

coreConcept: Achalasia due to absence of the myenteric plexus
statement: Absence or degeneration of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus of the esophagus most directly produces which disorder?
optionExplanations: Gastroesophageal reflux disease: Gastroesophageal reflux usually results from an incompetent lower esophageal sphincter rather than failure of sphincter relaxation.
Achalasia is the correct answer.
Pyloric stenosis: Pyloric stenosis is obstruction at the gastric outlet and is unrelated to the esophageal myenteric plexus.
Peptic ulcer disease: Peptic ulcer disease is caused by mucosal injury, commonly involving Helicobacter pylori or NSAID use.
Zenker diverticulum: Zenker diverticulum is a pharyngoesophageal pulsion diverticulum caused by dysfunction near the upper esophageal sphincter.
citation:
B. Achalasia

Explanation

Why B is correct:
Achalasia is caused by degeneration of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric, or Auerbach, plexus, resulting in impaired lower esophageal sphincter relaxation and loss of normal peristalsis.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Gastroesophageal reflux disease: Gastroesophageal reflux usually results from an incompetent lower esophageal sphincter rather than failure of sphincter relaxation.

C. Pyloric stenosis: Pyloric stenosis is obstruction at the gastric outlet and is unrelated to the esophageal myenteric plexus.

D. Peptic ulcer disease: Peptic ulcer disease is caused by mucosal injury, commonly involving Helicobacter pylori or NSAID use.

E. Zenker diverticulum: Zenker diverticulum is a pharyngoesophageal pulsion diverticulum caused by dysfunction near the upper esophageal sphincter.

coreConcept: Formation of the portal vein behind the pancreatic neck
statement: The hepatic portal vein is formed by union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins behind which part of the pancreas?
optionExplanations: Head: The pancreatic head lies within the duodenal curve but is not the standard landmark for portal-vein formation.
Uncinate process: The uncinate process passes posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels.
Neck is the correct answer.
Body: The body lies anterior to major retroperitoneal vessels farther to the left.
Tail: The tail approaches the splenic hilum.
citation:
C. Neck

Explanation

Why C is correct:
The superior mesenteric and splenic veins unite posterior to the neck of the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Head: The pancreatic head lies within the duodenal curve but is not the standard landmark for portal-vein formation.

B. Uncinate process: The uncinate process passes posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels.

D. Body: The body lies anterior to major retroperitoneal vessels farther to the left.

E. Tail: The tail approaches the splenic hilum.

statement: During tonsillectomy, injury to which vessel is a classic cause of troublesome venous bleeding from the tonsillar bed?
optionExplanations: Facial artery: The facial artery gives a tonsillar branch, but the classic venous hazard named in the tonsillar bed is the external palatine vein.
External palatine vein is the correct answer.
Lingual artery: The lingual artery lies deeper and is not the characteristic vessel injured in routine tonsillectomy.
Retromandibular vein: The retromandibular vein lies within the parotid region.
Superior thyroid artery: The superior thyroid artery supplies the upper thyroid and adjacent laryngeal structures.
citation:
B. External palatine vein

Explanation

Why B is correct:
The external palatine, or paratonsillar, vein descends from the soft palate near the lateral surface of the palatine tonsil and may cause significant bleeding during tonsillectomy.

statement: The epithelial component of the pancreas develops from buds arising from which tissue?
optionExplanations: Neural crest: Neural crest contributes to enteric neurons but not pancreatic epithelium.
Surface ectoderm: Surface ectoderm forms epidermis and related structures.

Intermediate mesoderm: Intermediate mesoderm forms much of the urogenital system.
Splanchnic mesoderm: Splanchnic mesoderm contributes connective tissue and vasculature, not the glandular epithelium.
citation:
C. Endodermal lining of the duodenum

Explanation

Why C is correct:
The dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds arise from endoderm of the caudal foregut, specifically the endodermal lining of the developing duodenum.

coreConcept: Bile duct as a posterior relation of pancreas
statement: Which structure is the most right-sided posterior relation of the head of the pancreas?
optionExplanations: Abdominal aorta: The aorta lies more centrally and posteriorly.
Inferior vena cava: The inferior vena cava lies posterior to the head but medial to the distal bile duct.
Splenic vein: The splenic vein runs behind the body of the pancreas, farther left.

citation:
D. Bile duct

The bile duct descends in a groove on, or may be embedded in, the posterior surface of the pancreatic head and is the most right-sided of the listed posterior relations.

coreConcept: Referred pain from a lower ureteric stone
statement: A ureteric stone produces colicky pain radiating from the loin through the groin to the penis. The radiation to the external genitalia most strongly suggests that the stone has reached which region?
optionExplanations: Renal pelvis: A stone in the renal pelvis more often causes flank discomfort without the full loin-to-groin pattern.
Upper third of ureter: Upper ureteric pain is usually felt mainly in the loin and upper abdomen.
Middle third of ureter: Middle ureteric pain may be referred toward the lower abdomen.

Major calyx: A calyceal stone may be asymptomatic or cause localized flank pain.

D. Lower part of ureter

As a stone descends into the lower ureter, pain commonly radiates to the groin, scrotum, or penis through spinal segments and nerves shared with the external genitalia.

statement: Damage to the sacral spinal cord segments or pelvic parasympathetic outflow is most likely to produce which type of urinary bladder dysfunction?
optionExplanations: Automatic bladder: An automatic bladder may develop after spinal shock when a cord lesion is above the sacral center and the sacral reflex arc remains intact.

Spastic bladder: A spastic bladder is associated more often with an upper motor neuron lesion above the sacral center.
Uninhibited neurogenic bladder: An uninhibited bladder follows loss of higher inhibitory control rather than destruction of the sacral reflex arc.

citation:
B. Atonic bladder

statement: During renal compensation for metabolic alkalosis, which process helps return extracellular pH toward normal?
optionExplanations: Increased bicarbonate excretion is the correct answer.
Increased hydrogen ion excretion: Increased hydrogen ion excretion would add new bicarbonate to blood and worsen alkalemia.
Complete bicarbonate reabsorption: Complete bicarbonate reabsorption preserves excess base.
Increased ammonium generation: Ammonium generation promotes net acid excretion and new bicarbonate formation.
Increased titratable acid excretion: Titratable acid excretion also increases net acid loss rather than base loss.
citation:
A. Increased bicarbonate excretion

When the body contains excess base, the kidneys can reduce bicarbonate reabsorption and increase urinary bicarbonate excretion, thereby lowering plasma bicarbonate and correcting alkalemia.

statement: Which metabolite is a potent allosteric activator of phosphofructokinase-1 in the liver?
optionExplanations: ATP: ATP signals a high-energy state and inhibits phosphofructokinase-1.
Citrate: Citrate is an allosteric inhibitor of phosphofructokinase-1.

Alanine: Alanine helps inhibit pyruvate kinase and supports gluconeogenic signaling.

Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate strongly activates phosphofructokinase-1 and inhibits fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase, favoring glycolysis over gluconeogenesis.

Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase: Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency causes classic galactosemia with jaundice, hepatomegaly, and E. coli sepsis.

Rickets: Rickets results from defective bone mineralization, usually due to vitamin D deficiency.

coreConcept: Metabolic alkalosis caused by loop diuretics
statement: Which acid-base disturbance is a common adverse effect of loop diuretics?
optionExplanations: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis is associated with diarrhea, renal tubular acidosis, and potassium-sparing diuretics.
High anion gap metabolic acidosis: High anion gap metabolic acidosis is not a typical direct effect of loop diuretics.

coreConcept: Reduced insulin secretion as a cause of polyuria

Desmopressin: Desmopressin is used for central diabetes insipidus, selected bleeding disorders, and uremic platelet dysfunction, not the chronic anemia itself.
Filgrastim: Filgrastim stimulates neutrophil production.
Vitamin K: Vitamin K corrects deficiency-related coagulopathy but does not replace erythropoietin.
Tranexamic acid: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic and does not stimulate erythropoiesis.
citation:
A. Erythropoietin

Explanation

Why A is correct:
Diseased kidneys produce insufficient erythropoietin, causing a typically normocytic anemia. Recombinant erythropoiesis-stimulating therapy promotes red-cell production after adequate iron status is ensured.

Why the other options are incorrect:

B. Desmopressin: Desmopressin is used for central diabetes insipidus, selected bleeding disorders, and uremic platelet dysfunction, not the chronic anemia itself.

C. Filgrastim: Filgrastim stimulates neutrophil production.

D. Vitamin K: Vitamin K corrects deficiency-related coagulopathy but does not replace erythropoietin.

E. Tranexamic acid: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic and does not stimulate erythropoiesis.

statement: Which of the following is a potassium-sparing diuretic?
optionExplanations: Furosemide: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that can cause potassium loss.
Hydrochlorothiazide: Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic that can cause hypokalemia.
Acetazolamide: Acetazolamide is a carbonic-anhydrase inhibitor and is not classified as potassium-sparing.
Spironolactone is the correct answer.
Mannitol: Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic.
citation:
D. Spironolactone

Explanation

Why D is correct:
Spironolactone antagonizes mineralocorticoid receptors in the collecting tubule, reducing sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Furosemide: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that can cause potassium loss.

B. Hydrochlorothiazide: Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic that can cause hypokalemia.

E. Mannitol: Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic.

statement: A stone completely obstructs a ureter. Which change is most likely to develop proximal to the obstruction?
optionExplanations: Hydronephrosis is the correct answer.
Renal agenesis: Renal agenesis is congenital absence of a kidney and is not caused by an acquired stone.
Horseshoe kidney: Horseshoe kidney is a congenital fusion anomaly.
Polycystic kidney disease: Polycystic kidney disease is inherited and is not a direct consequence of ureteric obstruction.
Renal ectopia: Renal ectopia is a congenital positional anomaly.
citation:
A. Hydronephrosis

Explanation

Why A is correct:
Ureteric obstruction causes back pressure with dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces, producing hydronephrosis and, if prolonged, renal parenchymal atrophy.

Why the other options are incorrect:

B. Renal agenesis: Renal agenesis is congenital absence of a kidney and is not caused by an acquired stone.

C. Horseshoe kidney: Horseshoe kidney is a congenital fusion anomaly.

D. Polycystic kidney disease: Polycystic kidney disease is inherited and is not a direct consequence of ureteric obstruction.

coreConcept: Pregnancy associated with a gravid uterus and hydronephrosis
statement: A gravid uterus with physiologic hydroureter and hydronephrosis is characteristic of which state?

Hyperthyroidism: Hyperthyroidism does not characteristically cause uterine enlargement with physiologic hydronephrosis.

A. Pregnancy

Pregnancy can cause physiologic hydroureter and hydronephrosis through mechanical compression by the gravid uterus and progesterone-mediated reduction of ureteric tone.

statement: Prominent U waves on an electrocardiogram are most characteristically associated with which electrolyte abnormality?
optionExplanations: Hyperkalemia: Hyperkalemia classically causes tall peaked T waves and, when severe, QRS widening.

Hypercalcemia: Hypercalcemia shortens the QT interval.

Why the other options are incorrect:

statement: Which amino acid becomes nutritionally essential in classic phenylketonuria?
optionExplanations: Alanine: Alanine can be synthesized by transamination of pyruvate.
Tyrosine is the correct answer.
Glutamate: Glutamate can be synthesized from alpha-ketoglutarate.

Glycine: Glycine can be synthesized from serine and other precursors.
